science-ch1-l1: Light from some stars takes many years to reach us, so we see them as they were long ago.
science-ch1-l2: Bread gets fluffy because tiny yeast living things eat sugar and make gas bubbles.
Astronauts on the International Space Station have grown and eaten fresh lettuce in space.
Sound travels faster through water than through air.
science-ch1-l3: Ice floats on water, so ponds freeze from the top and fish can keep swimming below.
Water grows bigger when it freezes, which can crack a bottle left full in the freezer.
Glass is made by melting sand in a very hot furnace.
science-ch1-l4: An apple in a bag can make bananas ripen faster, because apples give off a special gas.
Indian scientist C. V. Raman studied how light travels through liquids and won a Nobel Prize.
science-ch1-l5: India's Mars spacecraft, Mangalyaan, reached Mars on its very first try.
Penicillin medicine was found when a scientist noticed mould killing germs in a dish.
Honey almost never goes bad, because it has very little water in it.
science-ch1-l6: Scientists from many countries worked together to take the first picture of a black hole.
An octopus can change its skin color to look like the rocks and plants around it.
Honeybees dance to tell other bees where to find flowers and how far away they are.
science-ch2-l1: The tailor bird sews leaves together with plant fibres to make a cosy nest.
Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make fruit.
Ganges river dolphins find food by making clicking sounds in muddy river water.
science-ch2-l2: Lotus flowers grow in muddy water, but their petals stay clean and dry.
Bamboo is not a tree. It is a giant grass.
Penguins cannot fly, but they are great swimmers in the sea.
science-ch2-l3: The banyan tree grows roots from its branches, and they become new trunks.
Potatoes are stems, not roots, so you can grow a new plant from one.
A coconut is a fruit, and the seed is inside it.
science-ch2-l4: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
Kingfishers dive headfirst into water to catch fish.
Flying fish can leap out of the sea and glide over the water.
science-ch2-l5: A camel's hump is made of fat, not water, which helps it survive in the desert.
Desert cactus has spines instead of leaves, which helps it hold water.
Polar bears have black skin under their white fur.
science-ch2-l6: Sea otters hold hands when they sleep, so they do not float away from each other.
Tiny animals called corals build reefs, which are homes for many fish.
The Ganges river dolphin finds food by making clicking sounds in muddy river water.
science-ch3-l1: Rice, wheat and millets are all grains, but they grow in different places because of the weather.
Kerala's food is full of coconut, because coconut trees grow well in its warm, wet climate.
science-ch3-l2: Long ago, people ground spices and grains by hand using a heavy stone called a sil-batta.
A chulha is a clay stove. Some people still use chulhas in villages today!
Your food can travel by train, truck or ship, so you can enjoy fruits from far away.
science-ch3-l3: Sugar is a carbohydrate, and your body turns it into energy very fast.
Protein is a building block for your body. Your hair and nails are made of protein!
Your body stores extra energy as fat, so it can save energy for later.
science-ch3-l4: Iodised salt has a little iodine in it, which keeps your thyroid gland healthy.
science-ch3-l5: Iodine turns starch blue-black. You can test a potato or bread this way!
A drop of oil on paper leaves a shiny, oily spot that does not dry away.
science-ch3-l6: Millets grow well in dry places, so they are a healthy food for many villages in India.
Food miles tell us how far food travels before it reaches your plate.
Your body needs different food as you grow, and even the amount you need can change with age.
science-ch4-l1: The word lodestone means leading stone. Old sailors used it to find their way.
Magnets stick to iron, but not to wood, plastic or paper.
science-ch4-l2: Some birds can feel Earth's magnet. They use it to find their way.
Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places many times over millions of years.
Earth's magnetic north is near the North Pole, but not exactly on it.
science-ch4-l3: A compass does not point to the Pole Star. It points to Earth's magnetic north.
Sea turtles use Earth's magnetic field to find their way across the ocean.
A compass needle can point north even in a dark room.
science-ch4-l4: Sailors in ancient China used magnetic compasses to find their way at sea.
Your phone has a tiny compass inside it. It helps maps show which way you face.
A compass needle still works when it is floating in water.
science-ch4-l5: Magnets can pull on each other through paper, wood and glass.
Doctors use strong magnets in MRI machines to see inside the body.
science-ch4-l6: Ferrofluid is a liquid that makes spiky shapes when a magnet is near.
Earth's magnetic field acts like a shield that protects us from space winds.
Giant magnets in scrapyards can lift cars and carry them away.
science-ch5-l1: Ancient Egyptians measured with the cubit, the length from their elbow to their middle fingertip.
Horses are still measured in hands today. One hand is 4 inches, a unit based on a human hand.
Long before rulers, people used their hands, feet and fingers to measure things.
science-ch5-l2: Long ago, people in India measured cloth using a unit called the gaj.
The metre was first based on the size of Earth, measured from the North Pole to the Equator.
science-ch5-l3: The metal tip at the end of a measuring tape moves a little, so it measures correctly.
Scientists can measure the Moon's distance by bouncing a laser off mirrors left there.
Surveyors use special tools to measure the height of tall mountains.
science-ch5-l4: The Sun rises in the east, and people have used it to find directions for thousands of years.
Maps use the Equator as a reference line for measuring how far north or south a place is.
science-ch5-l5: Earth spins around once every day, so you are always moving, even when you sit still.
Our whole solar system moves around the centre of the Milky Way galaxy.
Stars look still, but they are moving very fast through space.
science-ch5-l6: A pendulum clock keeps time by swinging back and forth at the same rhythm.
Clock hands move in circles, and the hour hand goes round twice every day.
science-ch5-exam: Bees do a special waggle dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
Plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air.
Most of your body is water, which helps carry food and oxygen around.
science-ch6-l1: Paper is made from wood and other plants, so trees help make your notebook.
More than 4,000 years ago, people in the Indus Valley baked clay into pots and toy carts.
science-ch6-l2: A pencil uses wood for its body, graphite for writing and rubber for erasing.
Rubber comes from the milky sap of rubber trees. Kerala in India grows many of them.
Glass can be melted and made into new glass again and again.
science-ch6-l3: Gold is so soft it can be beaten into sheets thin enough for light to pass through.
Diamond is the hardest natural material. It can scratch almost any other material.
Mica is a shiny mineral found in India. It is not a metal, but it sparkles like one.
science-ch6-l4: Some glass frogs have see-through skin on their bellies.
Snowflakes are clear like ice, but many snowflakes together look white.
science-ch6-l5: One litre of water weighs about one kilogram.
A balloon full of air is heavier than an empty balloon, because air has mass.
Oil floats on water because it is lighter than water for the same amount of space.
science-ch6-l6: Air is matter too, even though we cannot see it. It takes up space and has mass.
Scientists have found about 118 elements, the simplest kinds of matter.
Water can be ice, liquid or steam. It is the same stuff in three forms.
science-ch7-l1: A metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon in the same room. The metal takes heat from your hand faster.
Your skin has tiny separate spots that feel cold, warmth and touch. They are not all in one place.
If one hand is in ice water and the other in warm water, the same tap water feels different to each hand.
science-ch7-l2: Your body is usually about 37 degrees Celsius, even on a cold winter day in India.
A thermometer can show the temperature of a cup of hot chai, which is much hotter than your body.
science-ch7-l3: Your body temperature is a little lower in the morning than in the evening.
An ear thermometer can check your body temperature in just a few seconds.
Digital thermometers do not need liquid inside, so they are safer to use than old glass ones.
science-ch7-l4: Scientists have a special scale where the coldest possible temperature is called absolute zero.
The Kelvin scale is named after Lord Kelvin, a Scottish scientist, and it starts at absolute zero.
science-ch7-l5: Liquid in a thermometer goes up when it gets warm, because the liquid takes up more space.
Old thermometers used a silver liquid called mercury inside the glass tube.
science-ch7-l6: Ice water stays at 0 degrees Celsius until all the ice melts.
Warm air near the ceiling of a room can be warmer than the air near the floor.
Your warm hand can change a thermometer's reading, so keep the bulb in the water while you read it.
